rationale: A wins because it keeps the strongest technical story closer to the supplied facts: 'Figma Make turns design files into React — and squeezes the designer-developer handoff' is testable without pretending the code is production-ready. B is almost there, but 'Figma turns designs into shippable React code' commits the exact sin its own proof section warns against. Both sets overreach on the Adobe peg, but A's proof asks are cleaner and its refused angles are sharper founder medicine.
gaps_in_A: 'Figma's first big swing since the Adobe deal died' is not in the fact block. The update says the launch follows the collapse, not that this is Figma's first major post-deal move.

'a whole job boundary — is what's being automated' pushes the labor-impact claim harder than the facts support. Good angle, but it needs adoption or code-quality evidence before that sentence earns its lunch.

'buyer-side reporter can do math on' the 4M users and Fortune 500 claims risks implying paid-seat adoption from legacy company-stated metrics. A flags the source, but the math still needs a narrower buyer base.
The product/category angle misses competitor context. A skeptical dev-tools reporter will ask how Make compares with existing design-to-code tools before buying the category story.
gaps_in_B: 'Figma turns designs into shippable React code' overclaims. The supplied fact is 'working front-end code'; shippable is a production-quality claim B has not earned.

'Figma's first move after the Adobe deal died: ship, not sell' is too cute and unsupported. The fact block says the launch follows the Adobe collapse, not that it is the first move or a strategic response.

'category-creation' is inflated without competitor evidence. B later admits this with 'How does the generated code and design-to-code claim compare to existing tools,' but the headline frame still outruns the proof.
'first notable product push after the collapse' repeats the same unsupported Adobe-sequencing claim in the body. Caveating it later does not un-invent it.
